kit.name: ELEGOO UNO R3 Super Starter Kit

identity.manufacturer: Generic (widely second-sourced); the datasheet used here was published by ElecFreaks, one of the original documenters of this module
generic_equivalents: US-015/US-100 (similar ultrasonic modules, not always pin-identical)
identity.package: module (45mm x 20mm x 15mm green PCB with two silver ultrasonic transducer cans and a 4-pin header)

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A sensor that measures distance by sending a short click of sound too high to hear and timing the echo, like a bat.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Measuring how far away an object or wall is, for example in an obstacle-avoiding robot or a parking-sensor project.
function.how_it_works_briefly: The Arduino sends the sensor a brief 10-microsecond 'go' pulse on the Trig pin. The sensor then sends 8 pulses of 40 kHz sound (above human hearing) out of one transducer and listens for the echo with the other. It holds the Echo pin high for exactly as long as the round trip took, and the Arduino converts that time into a distance.

pinout.name: Trig
pinout.notes: Send a 10us HIGH pulse here to start a measurement

pinout.name: Echo
pinout.notes: Goes HIGH for a duration proportional to distance

pins.pin_1_identification: Reading the silkscreen left to right with the two round silver transducer 'eyes' facing away from you: VCC, Trig, Echo, GND. Confirmed in the ElecFreaks datasheet's own labeled photo.

electrical.absolute_max_voltage: not published in the datasheet checked; treat 5V as the intended supply and do not exceed it
electrical.max_current: not separately specified beyond the 15 mA working current in the datasheet checked

key_specs.ultrasonic_frequency: 40 kHz (the datasheet's own summary table lists this as '40Hz', almost certainly a typographical error, since the descriptive text on the same page states 'eight 40 kHz' pulses; 40 kHz is used here)

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Rectangular green PCB about 45mm x 20mm, with two round silver-mesh cylinders ('eyes') mounted side by side on top and a 4-pin header along the bottom edge.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Green PCB; 'HC-SR04' printed on the board near the two transducers; pin labels VCC/Trig/Echo/GND silkscreened next to the header.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: 'HC-SR04' printed on the PCB, plus small markings near each silver cylinder distinguishing transmitter from receiver.
easily_confused_with: A dome-shaped PIR motion sensor module (different shape, not applicable here)
the RCWL-1601, a similar-looking single-PCB 'twin-eye' ultrasonic module that runs at 3.3V or 5V

example_connections.uno_pin: D9 (illustrative; any free digital output pin works)
D10 (illustrative; any free digital input pin works)

wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: None required (built-in pulseIn()); NewPing is a common optional convenience library

hazards: The two transducer cans are somewhat fragile; avoid pressing on the mesh
handling_notes: Connect GND before VCC when wiring on a live board, per the datasheet's own recommendation
Keep the sensing path clear of soft or absorbent materials (foam, cloth) which can swallow the echo and give false 'no object' readings
common_mistakes: Swapping the Trig and Echo wires
Testing against a surface smaller than about 0.5 square meters or at a steep angle, which the datasheet notes can produce bad readings
Powering it from 3.3V, below its rated 5V supply

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Always reads 0 or a max-range/garbage value
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Trig and Echo wires swapped, or GND not connected
symptoms_and_causes.check: Verify wiring against the VCC-Trig-Echo-GND order and confirm GND continuity with a multimeter

symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Target surface too small, soft, or angled; measuring faster than the recommended cycle
symptoms_and_causes.check: Test against a flat hard wall at close range and add at least 60ms between measurements

symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Dead sensor, no 5V present, or trigger pulse too short
symptoms_and_causes.check: Confirm 5V at VCC with a multimeter and confirm the code sends a pulse of at least 10 microseconds

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With the module powered, measure DC voltage between VCC and GND to confirm 5V is present. Trig and Echo are pulsed signals rather than steady levels, so a multimeter will mostly read close to 0V on them at rest; an oscilloscope is needed to see the actual pulses, though the multimeter is still useful to rule out a wiring fault.

confidence.notes: The datasheet's own specs table lists 'Working Frequency: 40Hz', which conflicts with its own descriptive text ('eight 40 kHz' pulses) a few lines earlier; I used 40 kHz as correct since it matches the well-established behavior of this sensor and the source's own prose.
